Many believe that bias against women
lingers in the business world, particularly
when it comes to evaluating their
leadership. Recently we had a chance to
see whether this assumption was true. In
a study of thousands of assessments
collected by the executive education
Program of international business school
insead, we looked at whether women
actually received lower ratings than men.
Our research drew on evaluations of 2,816
executives from 149 countries enrolled in
executive education courses at Insead.
The managers filled out self-assessments
and also invited subordinates, peers,
supervisors, suppliers and consumers to
evaluate them on a set of leadership
dimensions. As we looked for patterns
Within this data, we focused on
differences between the male and female
leaders, both in terms of how they saw
themselves and in terms of how the
observers evaluated them.
The first Surprise for us, given prior
Published research, was that we found no
evidence of a female ‘modesty effect’.
Quite the Opposite: Women rated
themselves significantly higher than men
rated themselves on four of the ten
dimensions. Our analyses of how leaders
were rated by their male and female
associates — bosses, Peers and
subordinates — also challenged the
common wisdom. Again, based on Prior
research, we had expected gender

As we sought to understand why
women fail to impress with their vision,
research from prior studies was not much
help. To begin with, most attempts to
compare men's and women’s styles have
focused on how leaders are rated by
subordinates. Yet, as we all know,
leaders play a key role in dealing with
people above, across, and outside their
units. Moreover, the vast majority of
studies ask participants either to rate
hypothetical male and female leaders or
to evaluate the ‘majority’ of male and
female leaders they know, rather than the
actual specific leaders they know well.
